messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 54
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Parole Officer
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 68

He is a 54-year-old Latin American man who has spent most of his adult life working around other people’s crises. As a parole officer, he is used to tense conversations, cramped interview rooms, and the constant effort of reading danger before it fully appears. For years he has told himself that staying calm is part of the job. His wife says he used to come home tired but still present, able to sit at the table, joke with her, ask about the grandchildren, and fall asleep with the television on low.

The change begins after an incident two years ago, on an afternoon that he still replays in fragments rather than as a complete memory. He is accompanying local police on a compliance check for a man on his caseload. The neighborhood is familiar to him, and the visit at first feels routine. The parolee is frightened but cooperative. What escalates things is not anything the man does, at least not in the way he remembers it. One of the officers starts shouting, then shoves the man against a wall. He remembers stepping forward and saying, “He’s complying,” with one hand half raised, trying to slow things down. The officer turns on him with a hard stare, calls him a traitor, and tells him to back off. Then there is a blur of motion—another officer grabbing his arm, twisting it behind his back, pushing him face-first onto the hood of a car.

What stays with him most is not the pain, though he feels that too. It is the shock of being treated like a threat by men whose uniforms he has worked beside for years. He hears someone yelling, hears himself trying to explain who he is, hears metal clatter and radios crackle. He cannot breathe right. For a moment he thinks they might actually shoot him. He remembers the hot pressure of the car hood against his cheek and the smell of dust and engine oil. After several minutes, when a supervisor arrives and the confusion clears, no one apologizes directly. There is muttering, paperwork, avoidance. He drives home with shaking hands and tells his wife only that “something happened.”

After that day, his body begins reacting before his mind can catch up. He startles at sirens so violently that his shoulders lock. If he sees patrol cars in his rearview mirror, his heart pounds and his mouth goes dry. At work he becomes watchful in a way that feels different from professional caution. He studies officers’ hands, their posture, their tone. During joint visits he positions himself near exits. He starts making excuses to avoid field work with police altogether, trading assignments when he can, then lying about why. He tells coworkers he is dealing with blood pressure issues.

Sleep changes first and worst. He wakes at 3 a.m. with his jaw clenched and his T-shirt damp, certain for a few seconds that someone is pinning him down. Sometimes he dreams of trying to speak and having no voice come out. Sometimes the dream is only pressure, heat, and the certainty that he is about to die. His wife reaches for him in bed and he jerks away before he knows it is her. He is ashamed every time. He begins sleeping on the couch “so I don’t wake you,” but both of them know that is not the full reason.

He also becomes angry in ways that scare him. At the office, if a younger officer jokes dismissively about “perps” or “resisting,” he feels a surge of heat so intense that he has to leave the room. Once, when a colleague casually says, “You know how these takedowns go,” he slams a file on his desk so hard that everyone goes silent. At home he is more withdrawn than explosive, but the distance is its own injury. His wife asks what he is thinking, and he says “nothing” because the truth feels impossible to explain. He no longer goes with her to family barbecues if he knows any law enforcement relatives will be there. He sits with his back to walls in restaurants and scans every entrance without meaning to.

He tells himself he should be over it. He was not shot. He was not hospitalized. Other people have suffered worse. But the humiliation clings to him, along with a deeper disorientation: the men he once trusted to share his sense of purpose made him feel helpless, disposable, and unsafe. He notices that he has begun doubting his own judgment. Paperwork takes longer because he rereads everything. He loses track during client meetings when a raised voice pulls him back into that afternoon. Certain smells—gasoline, hot metal—turn his stomach instantly.

Now, in his fifty-fourth year, he speaks carefully about what happened, as if the memory is edged and heavy. He still goes to work, still dresses neatly, still tries to be the steady one. But his world has narrowed. He avoids, scans, startles, and endures. He says the hardest part is that before that day he believed he knew where danger came from. Now it can come wearing the same badge he once saw as protection, and his body no longer lets him forget it.
